note: The estate's history as a timeline, retold in this record's own words from the concise history printed on The Park Map, Fourth Edition, by Douglas de Havilland, which he gave to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association. The facts are his; the sentences are not, because reproducing a man's own prose on a public page is a different thing from drawing on his research. The raw transcript stays in history_park_map_dougal.json, where the wording IS his, so the two can always be compared. Entries marked incomplete are ones where the map's column wrapped and the PDF's text layer lost the rest — they are shown as unfinished rather than completed from guesswork, and a task asks for them to be read off the original.
source: The Park Map, Fourth Edition, designed by Douglas de Havilland and donated to the Nottingham Park Residents' Association. Retold, not reproduced.

entries.text: Saxon settlers arrive and pass the sandstone rock by, putting their settlement instead on the ground where St Mary's church and the Lace Market stand today.
William the Conqueror, seeing the rock, orders a castle raised on it by his son Peverel. The woodland beside it is enclosed.
entries.why: The map's line breaks after the enclosure of the woodland; what the enclosure was for is lost.

entries.text: Nottingham receives its Great Charter, and from this point answers to nobody below the King.
Richard III is said to have mustered his troops in the Deer Park, marching them over the King's Meadow and away to Bosworth.
Charles I stays at Thurland Hall rather than the castle, which by now is reckoned unfit for a king.
Charles raises his standard on the ground now called Standard Hill. The town stays loyal to Parliament.
entries.why: The sentence stops at "the ensuing Civil" — the war itself is cut off.

entries.text: With the war over, Colonel Willoughby has the castle pulled down, to the considerable relief of a good many Nottinghamians.
The ruin is bought by William Cavendish, made 1st Duke of Newcastle three years later for the support he gave the King in the war.
Work starts on an Italianate palace on the site, at a cost of £14,000. The Duke dies before it is finished.
Queen Anne, second daughter of James II, comes to the throne. As Princess Anne she had lived at the Mansion House.
entries.why: The text layer breaks down here into "ottin 1 M", so the end of the entry is unreadable.

entries.text: The Duke leaves no son, and the title is recreated for his nephew Thomas Pelham, later Pelham-Holles, as 1st Duke of Newcastle.
entries.why: A stray letter ends the line in the transcript, so a few words are probably missing.

entries.text: No male heir again. The dukedom is recreated a second time, for the nephew Henry Pelham Clinton, who becomes the 2nd Duke.
The last of the great balls is held at the ducal mansion, given by the Duke, who was Earl of Lincoln as well.
The old castle fishponds are filled in with spoil dug out for the Cavalry Barracks.
entries.why: The entry breaks after "being", so where the barracks stood is not given.

entries.text: Henry Clinton dies and his son Thomas succeeds as 3rd Duke.
The 3rd Duke dies at forty-two, after a whooping cough treatment that went badly wrong, leaving a widow of thirty-five.
entries.why: The line stops at the Duchess's age; what followed for her and the estate is missing.

entries.text: The Dowager marries again, and sells land on Standard Hill to provide for the young Duke.
The first national census puts Nottingham at close to thirty thousand people.
entries.why: The comparison with 1821 is cut off after "will exceed".

entries.text: The 4th Duke, twenty-two years old, marries the heiress Georgina Elizabeth Munday of Shipley in Derbyshire.
entries.why: What the marriage added to the estate is lost after "adds".

entries.text: William Stretton builds St James's Church on Standard Hill. A nurses' home will replace it in 1936.
St Mary's Vicarage goes up on Standard Hill — the first building anywhere in what was then the Park.
Regency House is built at 2 Ropewalk, and is the oldest house standing in The Park today.
The 4th Duke, who is not popular, proposes developing the Park as a residential quarter. The proposal is resented.
entries.why: The line breaks after "resented by the" — by whom is not recorded here.

entries.text: Rioters set the Duke's mansion alight, provoked by his vote against the Reform Bill.
Fifty large houses now stand around the edge of the Park, built in the face of local opposition.
entries.why: The entry runs on past "the Park" and is cut.

entries.text: The 4th Duke dies. His son, Lord Lincoln, is held in far better regard by the town and its council than his father ever was.
T. C. Hine oversees the restoration of the burnt mansion, and the Corporation takes the building on.
entries.why: What the Corporation did with it is cut off after "rents the building".

entries.text: Nearly four hundred houses have been built, for the most part for wealthy and influential Nottingham men — A. J. Mundella among them.
Queen Victoria makes Nottingham a city, in the year of her Diamond Jubilee.
After 277 years in the family, the 8th Duke sells the Park to Oxford University, the purchase made through Lord Nuffield.
Clumber Park passes to the National Trust. The house there had been pulled down in 1938 to raise money.
Years of work by the Park Residents' Association, with the lawyer John Hallam leading it, come to fruition.
entries.why: The entry breaks at "bring to fruition the Nottingham" — almost certainly the Nottingham Park Estate Act, but the map's own words stop there.

entries.text: The 10th Duke dies and the dukedom of Newcastle becomes extinct.
The estate's records are moved from Oxford to the University of Nottingham.
